Still, the work of Flourens was very influential, and localization of brain function became a controversial topic, with many people holding strong opinions despite a continued lack of solid evidence one way or another. Then, in April 1861, a patient by the name of Louis Victor Leborgne came under the care of physician Paul Broca (whom we already met above in the section about trepanation). Leborgne had been hospitalized for the previous 10 years, stemming from epilepsy that started in his youth and had eventually led, by the age of 30, to aphasia—an inability to speak

. By the time Broca saw him, Leborgne was known as “Tan,” as this was essentially the only word he could say, often repeated twice in a row. Leborgne’s mind otherwise appeared intact—he could understand what was said to him and answer questions with gestures. At the time, in France, there were active discussions about whether there was a cortical locus for speech. Years earlier, physician Jean-Baptiste Bouillaud had described patients with anterior lobe damage who had trouble generating speech. Furthermore, a few days before Leborgne came under Broca’s care, at a Paris scientific meeting, physician Simon Auburtin, Bouillaud’s son-in-law, discussed a patient of his who had a skull opening over the anterior lobe due to a gunshot wound: “During the interrogation the blade of a large spatula was placed on the anterior lobes; by means of light pressure speech was suddenly stopped; a word that had been commenced was cut in two. The faculty of speech reappeared as soon as the compression ceased.
” Leborgne died a few days after coming under Broca’s care and an autopsy revealed significant damage to the frontal cortex in the left hemisphere (

). Broca published this result to immediate enthusiasm from the medical and scientific communities, and a few years later published a follow-up paper with several additional people with aphasia, solidifying his claim of the left frontal cortex as the locus of speech generation

By the middle of the 18th century, the gross anatomy of the brain had been described in reasonable detail. Following Thomas Willis, work by anatomists across Europe such as Gennari, Pourfour du Petit, Rolando, Vicq-D’Azyr, and Gratiolet, gave rise to a clear and detailed picture of the brain as a complex organ with multiple distinct anatomical regions. But what was the substance making up the organ of thought, memory, and emotions? Early explorations with small, hand-held homemade microscopes (

) allowed the Dutch draper Antonie van Leeuwenhoek—who had started making his own microscopes to assess the quality of his fabrics—to examine countless biological specimens, including a cow optic nerve,

which was the first nervous tissue to be seen at high magnification. Although without methods to enhance contrast, the optic nerve must have looked fairly nondescript to van Leeuwenhoek, it was sufficient for him to remark that the nerve was not composed of a hollow tube, as had been claimed by Alcmaeon over a thousand years earlier in Greece.
Most of the physiological findings described above have been studied in ex vivo retinae (i.e. a retina in a dish). The real world introduces several additional challenges.

Amacrine Cells: The most diverse set of cells in the retina are amacrine cells17,21. These are, with a few exceptions, inhibitory interneurons which collect input from bipolar cells and in turn inhibit bipolar, ganglion and other amacrine cells. In some vertebrate species, amacrine cells comprise more than 50 different cell types, each exhibiting a unique anatomy, physiology, and gene expression profile 5. Some amacrine cells exhibit distinct both dendrites and an axon, however many have processes which act as both axon and dendrite. Attempts to generalize are difficult in the face of this diversity, however some trends have been observed: First, almost all amacrine cells are inhibitory neurons releasing either GABA or glycine onto their targets; Second, glycinergic amacrine cells tend to have narrow dendritic trees, and thus small receptive fields, whereas GABAergic cells tend to have broader dendritic trees and thus larger receptive fields30; Third, many amacrine cells release an additional neurotransmitter, which can be excitatory, but is more commonly a neuromodulator such as a peptide or catecholamine5,6.
The most ancient text mentioning the brain dates to about 1,600 BCE and is written in hieroglyphs. It’s a copy of a surgical treatise originally written some 1,400 years earlier
and is known as the Edwin Smith papyrus (

), named after the American Egyptologist who purchased it in 1862 from an antiquities dealer near Luxor. This papyrus describes 48 cases, mostly of severe physical traumas, along with treatment recommendations. Many of the cases involve head injuries, including the now famous case n. 20 which describes a man with a hole in his skull—likely the result of a blow to the head sustained on the battlefield—that exposed the cortical surface of his brain (

). The case description, titled Instructions concerning a wound in his temple, penetrating to the bone, (and) perforating his temporal bone, recounts the effects of applying pressure on the exposed brain: “… if thou puttest thy finger on the mouth of the wound… he shudder exceedingly.” However, instead of recommending a surgical procedure, the suggested treatment was, “Now when thou findest that man speechless, his [relief] shall be sitting; soften his head with grease, (and) pour [milk] into both his ears.”

Here, we’ll focus on four debates surrounding questions that lead to our current understanding of brain function: 1) Where is the mind? 2) Is there localization of function in the brain? 3) What is the fundamental functional unit of the brain? 4) How do neurons communicate with one another?

Despite Galen arguing that the mind arose in the parenchyma, or brain tissue, much attention would subsequently be given to the ventricles as possible nodes of the mind (as will be described in detail in the next section). However, it wasn’t until the 1800s that Marie Pierre Jean Flourens, in his efforts to disprove phrenology (see more on this below as well), resected various brain regions, largely from rabbits and pigeons, and showed somewhat specific behavioral impacts. He found that removing the cerebrum appeared to impair sensory perception and judgement, while removing the cerebellum seemed to impair equilibrium and coordination. Thus Flourens, despite remaining adamant that there was no localization of function within the cerebrum, firmly placed the mind in the brain

January 26, 1874. A 30-year-old woman, Mary Rafferty, is admitted to the Good Samaritan Hospital in Cincinnati

. She presents with a hole in her head due to a cancerous ulcer: “The skull itself is eroded and has disappeared over a space two inches in diameter, where the pulsations of the brain are plainly seen

). Mary comes under the care of Dr. Roberts Bartholow. He is intrigued by the emerging field of electrotherapy and—having read of the experiments of Fritz and Hitzig, and Ferrier—realizes that Mary’s skull opening could allow him test out electrical stimulation in the human brain. In particular, Bartholow wants to see if he can repeat the results from dogs and monkeys, and drive motor movements in human via brain stimulation. He also wants to test out lateralization of function, and dural vs. cortical excitability. Though he later described Rafferty as “not very well nourished and rather feeble-minded,” he nonetheless sought and received her consent to perform brain stimulation experiments through her cranial cavity

Jan Evangelista Purkyně (aka Purkinje) was one of the first to take advantage of these experimental conditions and described cerebellar cortex as containing large and tightly packed globular structures from which emerged short extensions. These would go on to be named Purkyně neurons

. It remained unclear, though, whether globules—a term first used by Gabriel Valentin, one of Purkyně’s students—and nerve fibers were connected in any way. Others, such as Robert Remak and Otto Deiters, began using other staining approaches to visualize fibers in brain and spinal cord sections. A posthumous publication from Deiters in 1865 revealed that there were in fact two types of fibers, the axis cylinder (axon) and protoplasmic processes (dendrites), that extended from what looked like cell bodies

). However, Deiters hypothesized that these processes were fused to those of other “cells.” The idea that neuronal processes fused (or anastomosed) was formalized by German anatomist Joseph von Gerlach in 1871 when he proposed that the brain is built from specialized cells with extended fibers that fused with one another, forming a giant nerve net or syncytium

. Various configurations were proposed for this syncytium: dendrites fusing with other dendrites, axons with other axons, and dendrites with axons. The reticular theory was widely accepted by biologists, even if it largely contradicted cell theory which had been formalized in 1839 by German anatomists Schwann, for animals, and Schleiden, for plants. Cell theory stated that all living organisms are made up of individual cells

, but it seemed logical to consider that the brain, capable of exceptional functions, should present an exceptional structure not dependent on individual cells doing individual things. It was natural to think that the brain, which required lightning-fast information flow across and between its various regions, could be organized as a giant net of “cells.”

Neurotransmitter release in photoreceptors and bipolar cells occurs at specialized presynaptic structures called synaptic ribbons, which permit fast and continuous vesicular release from these neurons that signal via graded potentials<sup data-sup='32'>32</sup>. Each active zone within a photoreceptor or bipolar cell axon terminal possesses a ribbon shaped organelle which is attached to the presynaptic membrane at its edges and tethers synaptic vesicles along its surface<sup data-sup='33'>33</sup>. The ribbon allows for a ~5-10-fold increase in the number of vesicles that can be docked at the active zone as compared to a conventional synapse<sup data-sup='32'>32,</sup><sup data-sup='33'>33</sup>. In response to depolarization and calcium influx into the axon terminal, vesicles move down the face of the ribbon like on a conveyor belt, being shuttled to the release site.

Wilder Penfield was born in Spokane, Washington in 1891. He obtained a Bachelor of Arts in Philosophy from Princeton before moving to Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar in the lab of Charles Sherrington, where he obtained a Bachelor of Science in Physiology. Penfield then completed medical training at Johns Hopkins University and apprenticed with Harvey Cushing
. Penfield took his first job as a neurosurgeon in New York City, where he started working with William Vernon Cone, who would remain his neurosurgical partner for most of his professional career

. While working with Cone to refine neurosurgical techniques, Penfield developed an interest in research related to epilepsy. As part of this endeavour, in 1924 he travelled to Spain—where he studied under Ramón y Cajal’s pupil Pio del Rio-Hortega—to learn methods for studying glial cells, which allowed him to examine glial tumours and brain scars

Upon being asked why he decided to specialize in neurology, Oliver Sacks famously answered, “I became a neurologist rather than, say, a cardiologist, because there’s nothing for an intelligent man to be interested in in cardiology. The heart, I suppose, is an interesting pump, but it’s just a pump. Neurology is the only branch of medicine that could sustain a thinking man.”1 In this chapter, we provide a brief survey of ideas surrounding this most fascinating of organs, told through debates that helped frame our modern understanding of the brain. Descartes is often credited with popularizing the idea of dualism

—the idea that most of our bodily functions and capabilities arise from our corporeal being, but that our mind, or soul, arises in an ethereal, perhaps spiritual, manner. Even hundreds of years after Descartes’ death, such ideas continue to have traction, particularly in conversations surrounding the basis of consciousness
. Somewhat ironically, in death Descartes also came to embody the idea of separation of mind and body.

Galen had less to work with when it came to assigning mental faculties to specific parts of the brain. As such, while he split the mental faculties into three components—imagination, reasoning, and memory—he did not propose specific brain locations where these were processed. That task would be taken up by Christian Church Fathers of the 4<sup>th</sup> century CE. They took these faculties and assigned each to a different ventricle in the brain. Since brain activity was thought to arise via pneuma or spirits (i.e., some type of air-like substance) flowing through nerves, the ventricles seemed like a good place for the pneuma to be stored and work their magic. This theory, referred to as the cell doctrine or ventricular theory, would persist in variations—some with more ventricles, some with different functions assigned to different ventricles—for the next thousand years

). In general, sensory signals were thought to be received by the most frontal ventricle. From there, pneuma would be passed onto the middle ventricle for mental processing, and then the pneuma would pass to the most anterior ventricle for mental storage.

On the first day of experiments, Bartholow had some initial success. Cortical stimulation provoked contralateral limb movements. To “develop more decided reactions,” Bartholow turned up the current, but this caused clonic spasms in Rafferty’s arm, emotional distress and crying. Rafferty then lost consciousness, during which time she exhibited convulsions. After recovering—still on this first day of experiments—Bartholow continued with stimulations, though at a lower current. A couple days later, Bartholow met again with Rafferty to continue with experiments. Her health, however, was in decline, and so the day’s activities were postponed. The following day, her condition was “decidedly worse.” She died soon afterwards, and Bartholow went on to publish a paper on his results
. This was the first documented evidence of electrical stimulation of the human brain driving motor activity, but it drew considerable ethical concerns and Bartholow publicly sought to defend himself

. It would be many years before electrical stimulation of the human brain picked back up, this time paired with resections related to epilepsy patients, pioneered by the likes of Otfrid Foerster, Harvey Cushing and Wilder Penfield.

As outlined in the phototransduction section, photoreceptors encode only a limited range of luminance change about a mean in their membrane potential. At the level of ganglion cells, this means that a given ganglion cell’s firing rate is not an absolute measure of light intensity. Instead, firing rate represents a relative increase or decrease from the mean luminance. In fact, a given ganglion cell is only able to reliable signal increases in a spot’s intensity over about two orders of magnitude. However, through various mechanisms, the retina as a whole is able to adapt to the mean luminance of a given environment, meaning that the luminance response curve of a ganglion cells can shift depending on mean luminance, allowing us to see over roughly 10 orders of magnitude. However, light adaptation is not instantaneous, and can account for why it might take a minute for your retina to adjust when you pass between two environments with significantly different mean luminance levels (like walking from a dark room into a sunny environment).

blocks.content: A cataract arises when the lens becomes cloudy3. Cataracts arise relatively commonly as humans age, though they can also have genetic or lifestyle-related causes (eg. smoking, extended sun exposure, etc.). The extent of visual impairment caused by cataracts are wide ranging, from mild to completely obstructing the ability to focus images on the retina. Left untreated, it is a progressive issue. Cataracts can also arise in children, and if left untreated for extended period of time (especially if present throughout the critical period), can effect vision even once removed. The first cataract surgical procedures were documented in India around 1000 BC (in which the lens was pushed out of the way, so as not affect incoming light), and the first cataract removal procedure appeared in Egypt around 1000 AD. Currently, the standard protocol is to replace the cataract with an artificial lens, or simply remove the lens. Both approaches eliminate accommodation, but artificial lenses can be multifocal, to help correct for this.

As you may appreciate by this point, the history of neuroscience is littered with debates in which, to at least some extent, people on each side of the dispute were often both partly right and partly wrong. Furthermore, topics that once seemed settled can become highly contested when additional findings come to light. Nonetheless, with a combination of critical thinking and clever experimentation, over time we can slowly approach a correct understanding of how the brain works. Or, as the physiologist and visual scientist Selig Hecht once wrote, “If one can succeed in bringing a number of scattered phenomena into orderly arrangement, one decreases by so much the welter of unrelated facts that constitutes the present literature.

Despite his contrarian view, Golgi’s contributions to biology were innumerable. In addition to the staining method he invented, he and his students and staff at the University of Pavia (
) made several remarkable observations, describing, for example, the muscle-associated spindle essential for proprioception (Golgi tendon organ)
and the Golgi apparatus

In fact, looking at unstained brain tissue under a microscope, it is nearly impossible to visualize individual neurons, which are densely packed within tangles of ultra-thin dendritic and axonal processes. This limited initial progress in brain research after the development of the first microscopes. These obstacles, which also included difficulties in tissue handling (softness, degradation) and processing (sampling for microscopy), were gradually resolved during the 19th century. First, chemical solutions, from alcohol, to balsamic concoctions, to formaldehyde (the latter being still commonly used in neuroscience research) were increasingly employed to stop tissue degradation and harden fresh tissue samples, making brain matter easier to process for microscopy
. Second, the development of a precise instrument for tissue cutting, the microtome, allowed for consistent sectioning of brain tissue that could then be mounted on glass slides
. Third, various pigments and dyes, such as carmine or cresyl violet, were found to be efficient contrasting agents, revealing for the first time the brain’s myriad building blocks
. Lastly, refinements in compound microscopes, initially invented by Robert Hooke in the mid-17th century, permitted observations of brain tissue with increasing clarity.

“It is thus with regard to the disease called Sacred [epilepsy]: it appears to me to be nowise more divine nor more sacred than other diseases, but has a natural cause from the originates like other affections… They who first referred this malady to the gods appear to me to have been just such persons as the conjurors, purificators, mountebanks, and charlatans now are, who give themselves out for being excessively religious, and as knowing more than other people. Such persons, then, using the divinity as a pretext and screen of their own inability to afford any assistance, have given out that the disease is sacred, adding suitable reasons for this opinion, they have instituted a mode of treatment which is safe for themselves, namely, by applying purifications and incantations, and enforcing abstinence from baths and many articles of food which are unwholesome to men in diseases… But this disease seems to me to be no more divine than others; but it has its nature such as other diseases have, and a cause whence it originates, and its nature and cause are divine only just as much as all others are, and it is curable no less than the others, unless when, the from of time, it is confirmed, and has became stronger than the remedies applied. Its origin is hereditary, like that of other diseases… But the brain is the cause of this affection, as it is of other very great diseases.”

In contrast to the example above where an anatomical structure present in non-humans was mistakenly assigned to humans, during the heated academic debates following the release of Darwin’s On the Origins of Species, the inverse situation arose: a controversy about whether a certain brain structure was specific to humans and thus differentiated us from the rest of the animal kingdom. The year was 1858 and Richard Owen, Hunterian professor at the Royal College of Surgeons and superintendent of the British Museum, published a paper claiming that three parts of brain anatomy clearly distinguished humans from other primates. It seems likely that he was aware that Darwin’s book was about to be published and he wanted to get in front of it with a win for the anti-evolution side. In contrast to Linnaeus, Owen went so far as to put humans in an order of the phylogenetic tree all by themselves

. Owen’s claims were: 1) only in humans does the posterior part of the cerebrum (i.e., the caudal-most part of cortex) extend beyond and thus cover the cerebellum; 2) only humans have a posterior horn in their lateral ventricle; 3) only humans have a hippocampus minor (a structure now referred to as the calcar avis). The problem was that Owen—despite other important contributions to knowledge and the public dissemination of knowledge via his work at the British Museum—was wrong on each of these fronts. It seems that Owen largely based his conclusions on a belief that humans were superior to other animals, and a misreading (possibly purposefully so) of the scientific literature. Over the next years, “Darwin’s Bulldog” Thomas Huxley, then professor of General Natural History at the Government School of Mines pursued a single-minded take-down of Owen over these claims. Across several publications, Huxley and other like-minded scientists performed numerous dissections comparing human and non-human primate brains, outlining that each of Owen’s three claims were incorrect, and showing that the hippocampus minor was not unique to humans

In rodents, a group of neuroblasts compose a sheet at the back surface of the growing eye-cup. These cells have an I-beam shape when viewed in cross section, with anchors at the outer and inner margins of the developing retina. The nuclei within these cells undergo an interkinetic migration, shuttling between the inner and outer margins of the retina, during which time they also generate daughter cells that will go on to become the various retinal classes. Retinal ganglion cells and amacrine cells are born first, bipolar cells next, and photoreceptors last. Current evidence indicates that within a neuron class, each subtype is generated randomly – for instance, neuroblasts generating only direction-selective ganglion cells have not been found<sup data-sup='101'>101</sup>. The generation of different neuronal classes happens over a range of days, and newly generated neurons must migrate to their final positions. The temporal delay in generation of different neuronal classes complicates the retinal wiring process, as the dendrites and axons of synaptic partners arrive asynchronously in the plexiform layers. To solve this problem, the retina relies on a stereotyped set of genetically defined adhesive cues that guide retinal circuit assembly<sup data-sup='102'>102</sup>.

Horizontal cells: Horizontal cells modulate signals passing between photoreceptors and bipolar cells via feedback to photoreceptors (and possibly feedforward signals to bipolar cells). While these were the first retinal neurons whose light responses were measured with intracellular recording – by Gunner Svaetichin in the 1950s – many details about how they contribute to retinal processing remain unresolved.

Color opponency: First described in horizontal cells of fish by Gunner Svaetichin62, color opponency arises when a cell receives competing signals generated by visual stimuli of different wavelengths. In the primate retina, at the level of ganglion cells, it is generally believed that color opponency is split along red-green63 and blue-yellow64 axes. Red-green opponency is thought to be computed in midget ganglion cells, some of which exhibit a biased spectral sampling within their receptive field centers to either red or green cones65. In contrast, blue-yellow opponency is thought to be computed by small bistratified ganglion cells64, as well as type of widefield ganglion cell66. While the exact role of color opponency in the retina remains an area of active research67, signals from color opponent ganglion cell types appear to make their way to color-coding visual regions in the brain, which eventually lead to color perception68.
